Neither number. The premise isn't right: more agents don't always give better results, and for your budget they often give worse ones.

It's tempting because a team of specialists sounds better than one generalist. But an agent isn't a free worker. Every agent is its own loop of model calls, and each call re-sends its instructions and context, so you pay for tokens again each time. Every handoff between agents is also a chance to lose detail. Picture a car where each gear has its own separate driver, and they have to radio each other before every shift.

**A split pays off when:**
- The subtasks need very different tools or instructions, so one prompt gets crowded.
- A subtask has a long, noisy context, like a 200-page manual, that you want kept out of the main conversation.
- Subtasks are independent and can run in parallel.

**A split doesn't pay off when:**
- The steps depend on each other in a fixed order. A plain workflow does that cheaper and more predictably.
- The agents would need to share most of the same context.

For your assistant, one agent with three tools is the sensible default: manual search, calendar check, booking. Add a second agent only if you can name the specific problem it solves, such as manual lookups bloating the context. That is also the argument you can defend at your design review.

You haven't had a lesson on multi-agent systems yet. I can write one, starting with a hands-on comparison of one agent against several on a request like "book the laser cutter Friday".

Quick check: a student asks "Is the laser cutter free Friday?" Would you need a second agent for that, and why or why not?
